# ¿Estoy expuesto? / Am I Exposed?

> Free tool that checks whether an email address or a password appears in known
> data breaches, and then explains in plain language what to change first.
> Available in Spanish and English. No account is needed to run a check, email
> addresses are not stored, and passwords are checked with k-anonymity: only the
> first five characters of a SHA-1 hash ever leave the browser, so the password
> itself is never sent anywhere. A paid report adds a personalised action plan.

> Herramienta gratuita para revisar si un correo o una contraseña aparece en una
> filtración de datos conocida, con una explicación clara de qué hacer después.
> No pide cuenta, no guarda el correo, y la contraseña nunca sale del navegador.

## The tool

- [Am I Exposed?](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/): the checker itself. English is
  the default: the settlement data is United States litigation and the
  subscription is sold there.
- [¿Estoy expuesto?](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/es/): the same checker, in Spanish.

## Data breach settlements

A page per United States case, in English only, because these are U.S. lawsuits.

- [All settlements](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/settlements/): the index. 1,075
  cases, of which 768 reached a settlement and 307 are still in court. Each page
  gives the settlement fund, the maximum paid per person, the claim deadline and
  whether it has passed, who the class covered, what data was exposed, and a link
  to the court-appointed administrator's own claim site where one is on record.
- Browse by company name from A to Z at
  https://www.am-i-exposed.com/settlements/letter-a/ through
  https://www.am-i-exposed.com/settlements/letter-z/
- Example: [Neiman Marcus](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/settlements/neiman-marcus/),
  a $3.5 million fund paying up to $2,500 per person, claims closed 8 October 2025.

Sources are Top Class Actions and ClassAction.org, cross-referenced against Have
I Been Pwned so a visitor can be told which of these breaches holds their own
address. The catalogue is refreshed weekly. We are not lawyers, we take no fee
from any claim, and we never file on anyone's behalf: appearing in a breach is
not the same as being a member of the class.

## Written pages (Spanish)

- [Preguntas frecuentes](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/es/preguntas-frecuentes/):
  what happens to your email, how a password is checked without being seen, and
  what appearing in a breach does and does not mean.
- [Qué hacer si se filtró mi correo](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/es/que-hacer-si-se-filtro-mi-correo/):
  the seven steps in the order that matters, and the three things that do not help.
- [Cómo saber si mi contraseña fue filtrada](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/es/como-saber-si-mi-contrasena-fue-filtrada/):
  k-anonymity explained without jargon, and what the leak count actually means.
- [Política de privacidad](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/es/privacidad/)
- [Términos y condiciones](https://www.am-i-exposed.com/es/terminos/)

## Who runs it

- Operator: Selentic Group S.A.C., a cybersecurity company based in Lima, Peru.
  https://www.selenticgroup.com/
- Contact: info@selenticgroup.com
- Breach data: Have I Been Pwned (https://haveibeenpwned.com), used under its
  Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence.
- Price: checking an email address or a password is free, and reading any
  settlement page is free. The personalised action plan report costs S/ 19.00
  PEN in Latin America and US$ 5.00 in the United States, and includes 30 days
  of access. Settlement alerts are US$ 3.00 a month, United States only.
- Not to be confused with ami.exposed, am-i.exposed or "How Exposed Am I",
  which are different tools run by other people.

## What makes it different

Most breach checkers answer one question: were you in a breach, yes or no. This
one is built around the next question, which is what to actually do about it,
written for someone who is not a security professional.

And it answers a question almost nobody else writes down: when the company that
lost your data is made to pay, how much was it, until when could it be claimed,
and where. Claim rates on these settlements run below 10 percent and often below
1 percent, so most of that money is never collected.
